paras: The Bradley mill posse shooting was a pursuit and exchange of gunfire between a Mobile County sheriff's posse and a group of Black sawmill workers from Bradley, Alabama, on August 25-27, 1905. Officers said they fired on the men at Beaver Meadow after the men fired first, and a deputy believed he had hit one of them, though no wounded man was found. One man, Boston Moore, was jailed, and the man the Montgomery Advertiser called the ringleader, Dave Wells, was last reported hiding in a swamp.

Bradley was a sawmill flag station on the Mobile and Ohio Railroad just north of Oak Grove, about fifteen miles north of Mobile. T. N. Mashburn, described variously as the mill's manager, woods foreman or "team boss," told the sheriff on August 26 that he had discharged some Black workers the previous evening and that they had threatened to kill him. He said he had been told they had armed themselves with Winchesters and pistols and would kill him when he returned; an Associated Press report added a threat to burn the mill.

Deputy Cherry's account in the Birmingham Age-Herald traced the trouble to Friday, August 25, when four armed men entered the company store and one of them, Charles Denton, cursed a white man. In that account Mashburn remonstrated, the men cocked their guns in the store door and threatened the white men, and after being driven to a hill they fired on the store, whose occupants fired back.

On August 26 Deputy W. S. Brewster at Oak Grove wired Sheriff Powers that a "Riot" was "brewing" at Bradley, and the sheriff left by train that afternoon with three deputies and warrants for the men. Finding that the men had gone to a picnic at Beaver Meadow, further north in the county, the posse followed and, joined by Brewster, met three of them early that night. According to the posse, the three opened fire, the officers returned it, and Deputy Cherry was "positive he brought down one," who could not be found in the dark and was thought carried off by his companions.
At 1 a.m. three deputies went back to Bradley and searched "every negro shack on the hill," finding only one man, who was not wanted.

Brewster and a number of white men from Bradley and Beaver Meadow kept searching on August 27 and arrested Boston Moore, who was jailed in Mobile to answer three charges. Searchers found Dave Wells's hat, pierced by a bullet, along with his guitar and pieces of his shirt with holes "as if penetrated by buckshot," and the Age-Herald reported a bloodied shirt in the swamp. Wells was believed to be in Beaver Meadow swamp, and no report of his capture, of anyone's injury, or of a trial appears in the coverage.

The episode appeared only in white papers, over two days, and every account came from the mill boss or the officers. The Montgomery Advertiser's Mobile bureau gave it the fullest treatment, opening with the headline "Trouble Is Expected" and a deck saying the officers "May Kill a Few Would-be Assassins." Its follow-up said the posse had "scattered the belligerent negroes from Bradley" and counted two unrelated arrests of Black men taken off a train as "happy catches."

An Associated Press brief, "Negroes Threaten Manager of Plant," ran in the Richmond Times-Dispatch and in the Birmingham Age-Herald, which spelled the manager's name "Washburn." The Age-Herald's August 28 story, headlined "Officers Capture One Ringleader," relayed Deputy Cherry's version of the store confrontation in a flatter tone. No Black-press coverage of the episode was found.

The Advertiser placed the gunfire at Beaver Meadow on the night of August 26, while the Age-Herald described shooting at the Bradley store on Friday and said the sheriff went out "Friday night" and captured no one. The Advertiser's dated bureau reports put the sheriff's departure on Saturday afternoon, so the Age-Herald's store shooting may have been an earlier exchange rather than the posse fight. The papers also differed on Moore, a ringleader to the Age-Herald but, to the Advertiser, not among the men fired on.

reader.title: Bradley mill posse shooting
bases: A Mobile County sheriff's posse holding warrants pursued a group of armed Black mill hands after a dispute with a mill boss, exchanged gunfire with them and searched Black homes; no mob killing is reported (A1, A4, A6).

The Advertiser's Mobile bureau (A1, A4, A5), the Associated Press (A3) and a separate Age-Herald Mobile dispatch (A6) agree on the threats against Mashburn, the gunfire and Boston Moore's arrest, though they differ on when and where the shooting took place.

accounts.label: Mill boss and deputy (first report)
accounts.gist: Mashburn told the sheriff that men he had discharged threatened to kill him and had armed themselves with Winchesters and pistols; the AP added a threat to burn the mill.

accounts.label: Sheriff's posse (Advertiser bureau)
accounts.gist: Three of the men opened fire on the officers at Beaver Meadow; the fire was returned and Deputy Cherry believed he brought one down, who was likely carried off by comrades.

accounts.label: Deputy Cherry (Age-Herald)
accounts.gist: On Friday four armed men threatened the white men at the company store after Denton cursed one of them, then fired from a hill and the men at the store fired back; the sheriff's later search caught no one.

framing.detail: The Advertiser headlined 'Trouble Is Expected' and 'May Kill a Few Would-be Assassins', and later called the men 'belligerent negroes' the posse had 'scattered'.
The AP brief 'Negroes Threaten Manager of Plant' gave the threats with no details, noting no telegraph line to Bradley.
The Age-Herald's 'Officers Capture One Ringleader' relayed Deputy Cherry's account of the store confrontation.

conflicts.note: The Advertiser's dated bureau reports place the sheriff's departure on Saturday afternoon, so the Age-Herald's 'Friday night' for the posse looks mistaken; its store shooting may be a separate, earlier exchange that the Advertiser does not mention.
